parts.title: The volcano in the kitchen
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
Last year, I decided to enter our school science competition with a project about volcanoes. My plan was simple: I would build a model volcano in the garden and make it erupt with baking soda, vinegar and red food colour. I read about it online, I watched three videos, and I felt sure that nothing could go wrong.

On the day before the competition, I tested the volcano in the kitchen, because it was raining outside. My mother was at work, and I thought I would tidy everything up before she came home. I mixed the baking soda and vinegar, and a small red river began to run down the side. It looked wonderful. Then I decided that it was not big enough, and I added another cup of vinegar.

The next minute was a disaster. Red foam shot up to the ceiling, ran across the table and fell onto the floor. The dog, who had been sleeping in his basket, woke up and started to bark. When my mother arrived home, I was kneeling on the floor with a mop, covered in red from head to foot.

She was not angry, to my surprise, and she even helped me to clean up. Next day, I took a smaller volcano to school, and it worked perfectly. I came second, and the judges said that my explanation was the clearest. But the story that everybody remembers is the one about the kitchen.

questions.prompt: Why did the writer feel confident about her project?
options: She had a teacher to help her.
She had won a prize before.
She had won the contest before.
questions.explanation: She read about it online and watched three videos, so she felt sure nothing could go wrong.

questions.prompt: Why did she test the volcano in the kitchen?
options: She wanted her mother to see it.
Her mother had asked her to.
questions.explanation: She tested it in the kitchen because it was raining outside.

questions.prompt: What did she do that caused the problem?
options: She used too much baking soda.
She dropped the red food colour.
questions.explanation: She decided the volcano was not big enough and added another cup of vinegar.

questions.prompt: How did her mother react?
options: She was too tired to speak.
questions.explanation: She was not angry and even helped to clean up.

questions.prompt: What happened at the competition?
options: The judges laughed at the kitchen story.
The judges did not like the volcano.
questions.explanation: She took a smaller volcano, it worked perfectly, and she came second.

parts.title: The story of the light bulb
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There are three extra sentences.
parts.passage:
Today we take electric light for granted, but just 150 years ago, most people used candles or oil lamps in the evening. [1] The idea of a light bulb was not new, and many inventors had tried to make one.

In the 1870s, two men were working on the problem, one in England and one in the United States. [2] Their bulbs were very different from those we have now, and they did not last long.

The American inventor, Thomas Edison, tested thousands of materials to find the best thread for his bulb. [3] Finally, he found that a thin thread made of cotton and burned in a special way could give light for over a thousand hours.

However, a light bulb is not much use without electricity in the home. [4] It took many years before every town had power stations and wires to bring electricity to the houses.

Today, the old bulbs are being replaced by new ones, which are much cheaper to use. [5] Perhaps in a hundred years, our children will wonder how we managed with such wasteful lamps.
sentences: Edison also had to find a way to produce and supply the power.
His assistant later became rich by selling his own lamp.
A single modern bulb can last for twenty years.
Both of them came close to success.
Candles are still popular for birthday cakes.
It was the invention of the light bulb that changed this.
Some of his tests failed after only a few minutes.
The cost of a bulb was too high for most families.

gaps.explanation: "Most people used candles or oil lamps" is followed by the invention that changed this; the next sentence says the idea was not new.
Two men worked on the problem; "Both of them came close" continues, and the next sentence says their bulbs did not last long.
Edison tested thousands of materials; some failed within minutes, and "Finally" introduces the success.
A bulb needs electricity at home; the sentence about producing and supplying power leads to the many years before towns had power stations.
Old bulbs are being replaced by cheaper ones; a modern bulb lasting twenty years supports this, and the next sentence looks to the future.

Scientists are now trying to build robots that can help older people to live [4] their own homes for longer. They could carry heavy bags, remind people to take their medicine, or call for help if somebody [5]. However, many people worry that robots will take away jobs. Experts say that the best idea is to let humans and machines [6] together, so that each does what it does best.

questions.prompt: Gap 4

parts.title: An email to a teacher
parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage:
Dear Mr Hale,
I am writing to tell you about my project for the science fair. I would like to build a small machine [1] makes electricity from the wind. I have already bought most of the parts, but I still need [2] find a small motor. Could you tell me [3] there is one in the school lab? I would be very grateful if you could help, [4] I do not have much money. The fair is [5] the fifth of May, so I do not have much time. I promise to be careful, and I will wear goggles [6] all times.
Yours sincerely,
Winslow Pike

gaps.explanation: The relative pronoun refers to the machine.
"Need to find" is followed by the infinitive.
"Tell me if there is one" is an indirect yes/no question.
"Because" gives the reason why he needs help.
"At all times" is a fixed expression.

Leave it on the window for a couple of hours, then plug in your phone and see how much power it has collected. Call me if you have any problems. Good luck!

parts.title: A guide talks at a science museum
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note. Write one or two words, a number, a date or a time.

turns.speaker: speaker-1
turns.text: Hello, everyone, and welcome to the Discovery Science Museum. My name’s Gwendolen, and I will show you round this morning. We are going to begin on the ground floor, so please follow me. Many people think the tour starts at the top, in the dome, but we save that for the end of the visit, because it’s a long way up. On the ground floor, you’ll find the space hall. There are models of planets and a satellite, and a film about astronauts, but the thing I like best is a real rocket engine, which was used in the nineteen seventies. You can’t touch it, but you can stand very close. Next, we go up to the first floor, to the electricity room. Be careful, it is not dangerous, but it’s strange! If you hold the silver ball, the electricity makes your hair stand up. Some visitors want to try with a hat, but it doesn’t work, so please take your hats off. After that, we have the robot show. It was at ten, but it moved, and now it starts at eleven. It lasts about twenty minutes, and the robots are the stars. Then it’s time for lunch. We have a picnic area in the garden, but it’s raining today, so please use the café on the second floor. The sandwiches are good, and the soup is cheap. In the afternoon you can explore on your own. But I need to warn you about the labels. Green means you can touch, yellow means ask first, and the one to be careful about is red. Those objects are very fragile or very hot, so please don’t touch anything with that label. If you have any problems, ask anyone wearing a blue T-shirt. They’ll be happy to help. Right, are we ready? Let’s start our adventure.

gaps.prompt: The main exhibit in the space hall is a genuine ___ engine
gaps.explanation: There are models of planets and a satellite, but she likes best the real rocket engine.

gaps.explanation: Hats do not work; the electricity makes your hair stand up.

parts.title: An interview with an inventor
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Hildebrand, your bicycle light is sold in twenty countries. How did the idea start?

turns.speaker: hildebrand
turns.text: I’d love to say it came from a science lesson, but I was a bad student! And I don’t watch much television. No, one winter evening I was cycling home along a dark country road, my old lamp ran out of battery, and I couldn’t see anything. I nearly ended up in a ditch. I thought, why can’t a light make its own power?

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Was it easy to build?

turns.speaker: hildebrand
turns.text: Not at all. My first version worked, and it wasn’t expensive, I made it from parts in my garage. Nor was it hard to sell, a friend at work wanted one at once. The trouble was that it was big and very noisy, like a coffee grinder on your wheel. Nobody wanted a heavy lamp that sounds like that.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Did anyone help you to continue?

turns.speaker: hildebrand
turns.text: My sister did. My father thought it was only a hobby, and my old teacher said I should find a proper job. But my sister told me to carry on. She even tested the lights in the rain for me, and she never complained.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: How did you start the company?

turns.speaker: hildebrand
turns.text: A bank refused to lend me any money, and my parents didn’t have any to give. In the end, I entered a competition for young inventors and won second prize. A big company saw my light at the final and helped me to make it in a factory.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What do you enjoy most about the job today?

turns.speaker: hildebrand
turns.text: I’m lucky to travel to other countries, and I’ve met some famous people, which is fun. But my favourite thing, honestly, is when I’m in a city and I see a child riding with my light on the front. That makes me smile every time. It is a small thing, but it’s very special.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Do you ever think about stopping?

turns.speaker: hildebrand
turns.text: Never. There are always new ideas in my notebook, and my team is full of young people with energy. Working with them keeps me curious, and I learn something new every week.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What would you say to a young inventor?

turns.speaker: hildebrand
turns.text: Look around you, at ordinary life. Every small problem, like a broken umbrella, is a chance for an idea. Don’t copy other people, and you don’t need to study abroad, I never went to a university. Just be curious and keep trying, even when it goes wrong.
